81.event_title: The Rule of Saint Benedict orders that guests be received as Christ
81.event: Benedict of Nursia wrote his Rule for monks around 530, and it became the foundational rule of Western monasticism. Its chapter 53 directs that all guests who arrive be received as Christ himself, citing the gospel words about welcoming the stranger. It sets out how the abbot and community are to meet guests, wash their hands and feet, give special care to the poor and pilgrims, and keep a separate guest house and kitchen so that visitors can always be served.
81.explanation: Benedict built hospitality into the very structure of the monastic household, making the reception of guests one of the purposes the community existed to serve.
81.tie_back: The kural says the whole business of keeping a home exists in order to cherish guests, and the Rule organised an entire household, with its own guest house and kitchen, around that duty.
81._accuracy_note: A strong institutional parallel to the kural's claim, though a monastery is a religious community rather than the lay householder Valluvar addresses.

82.event_title: The villagers of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon shelter refugees
82.event: Led by Pastor Andre Trocme, his wife Magda and Pastor Edouard Theis, the people of Le Chambon-sur-Lignon and the surrounding plateau sheltered an estimated 5,000 people between 1940 and 1944, about 3,000 to 3,500 of them Jews. Refugees who arrived at the door were housed in private homes, farms, hotels and schools, and residents forged identity and ration cards for them; Pastor Trocme and Pastor Theis were arrested and held for 28 days in 1943. In 1990 Israel recognised the inhabitants collectively as Righteous Among the Nations.
82.explanation: In a time of scarcity and danger, an entire community refused to keep its food and shelter to itself while strangers were left outside.
82.tie_back: The kural says eating alone while a guest stands outside is not worth wanting even if the food were the elixir of life, and Le Chambon chose to share even its rations rather than turn strangers away.
82._accuracy_note: A powerful case of refusing to enjoy safety and food alone while strangers waited at the door, though the stakes were rescue rather than ordinary hospitality.

83.event_title: Guru Amar Das makes the free kitchen central to Sikh life
83.event: The Sikh langar, a free communal kitchen introduced by Guru Nanak, was strengthened by the third Guru, Amar Das, who made it a rule that anyone wishing to see him had first to eat in the langar, where all sit in rows as equals. The Mughal emperor Akbar is recorded as having eaten in the langar. The Guru ka Langar at the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar serves cooked food to visitors of any religion or background, day and night, with its costs met from temple funds.
83.explanation: The langar shows that feeding all comers every day can be sustained across centuries without exhausting those who provide it.
83.tie_back: The kural says the household that tends arriving guests day after day will never be worn down into ruin, and the langar has fed guests daily for generations without collapsing.
83._accuracy_note: A close illustration of habitual daily hospitality that has never ruined its hosts, though it is a community institution rather than a single household.

84.event_title: Gander takes in the passengers of 38 diverted airliners
84.event: When North American airspace was closed after the attacks of 11 September 2001, 38 airliners landed at Gander, bringing nearly 7,000 passengers and crew to a town of about 10,000 people. Residents housed the travellers in schools, halls and their own homes for several days, volunteers fed them, local businesses donated supplies and pharmacists filled prescriptions at no charge. The town was later honoured in Washington, and Lufthansa named one of its aircraft Gander-Halifax in recognition of the care given to passengers.
84.explanation: Gander's cheerful, open-handed welcome to thousands of strangers earned it lasting gratitude, honour and goodwill around the world.
84.tie_back: The kural says fortune comes to dwell gladly with the one who welcomes guests with a glad face, and Gander's warm welcome brought the town honour and lasting friendship.
84._accuracy_note: A good documented case of glad hospitality followed by honour and goodwill, though the reward was recognition rather than prosperity in the kural's sense.

85.event_title: The Choctaw Nation sends famine relief to Ireland
85.place: Choctaw Nation, Indian Territory (now Oklahoma), United States
85.event: In 1847, less than two decades after their forced removal from their homelands on the Trail of Tears, Choctaw people gathered and raised 170 dollars for the relief of the Irish famine. The money was sent through relief committees in the United States to help buy food for the starving in Ireland. The gift is still commemorated in both nations, including by the Kindred Spirits sculpture in County Cork and a Choctaw-Ireland scholarship.
85.explanation: A people who had themselves suffered dispossession gave from their own scarcity to strangers an ocean away, and the gift is still remembered as a bond between the two nations.
85.tie_back: The kural praises the one who feeds others first and lives on what remains, and the Choctaw gave to the hungry before attending to their own hardships.
85._accuracy_note: Next-best only: a documented act of giving to others first from scarcity, but it was distant relief rather than feeding guests at home, and the kural's promise of an unsown harvest is not shown.

86.event_title: The hospice of the Great St Bernard Pass is founded
86.event: Around 1050 Bernard of Montjoux, archdeacon of Aosta, founded a hospice at the summit of the Great St Bernard Pass to shelter and protect travellers crossing the Alps. Canons have lived there ever since, welcoming every traveller, and from the seventeenth century the monks kept dogs that helped them find travellers lost or buried in the snow. Bernard was later venerated as a saint and the pass and the dog breed bear his name.
86.explanation: The hospice community did not merely receive those who reached its door; it went out watching and searching for the travellers still on the road.
86.tie_back: The kural honours the host who cares for the departing guest while watching for the one still to come, and the St Bernard monks spent centuries tending travellers and looking out for the next.
86._accuracy_note: A strong image of hosts watching the road for coming guests, though the kural's reward of welcome among the heavenly can only be read in Bernard's later sainthood.

87.event_title: Lorenzo de' Medici takes the young Michelangelo into his household
87.event: Lorenzo de' Medici, ruler of Florence, opened a school of sculpture in his garden of San Marco, where the teenage Michelangelo attracted his attention. Lorenzo invited the boy to live in the Medici palace, where he was brought up like a member of the family, studied the Medici collection of ancient sculpture under Bertoldo di Giovanni and mixed with Lorenzo's circle of scholars. Michelangelo's early works such as the Battle of the Centaurs date from this stay, which ended with Lorenzo's death in 1492.
87.explanation: Lorenzo's hospitality to a gifted boy yielded a return far beyond anything he could have measured, through Michelangelo's later art.
87.tie_back: The kural says the fruit of hospitality cannot be fixed in advance but matches the worth of the guest, and the Medici household's guest turned out to be one of the greatest artists in history.
87._accuracy_note: A reasonable illustration of a guest whose worth determined the yield, though this was patronage of a pupil as much as hospitality to a visitor.

88.event_title: The fall of Heshen, the Qianlong emperor's favourite
88.event: Heshen rose from imperial bodyguard to the highest offices of the Qing state under the Qianlong emperor and amassed an enormous private fortune through corruption. When Qianlong died in February 1799, his son the Jiaqing emperor had Heshen arrested, stripped of all his posts and condemned to death, and his vast estate was confiscated. Official inventories of the seized wealth, possibly exaggerated by his enemies, listed huge quantities of silver, pawnshops, furs and gold.
88.explanation: A lifetime spent gathering and guarding wealth for himself ended with Heshen losing all of it at a single stroke.
88.tie_back: The kural says those who never took up the sacrifice of hospitality will one day lament that they toiled and saved and have nothing to hold on to, and Heshen's hoard was taken from him entirely.
88._accuracy_note: Next-best only: a documented case of hoarded wealth ending in total loss, but the sources tie his fall to corruption and politics, not to any failure of hospitality.

89.event_title: The voyage of the St. Louis
89.place: Havana, Cuba, and the Atlantic coast of the Americas
89.event: In May 1939 the liner St. Louis sailed from Hamburg carrying 937 passengers, almost all Jewish refugees from Nazi Germany. Cuba admitted only 28 of them and ordered the ship to leave, and the passengers' appeals to the United States and Canada were turned down. The ship returned to Europe, where Britain, the Netherlands, Belgium and France agreed to take the passengers; 254 of them were later killed in the Holocaust.
89.explanation: Wealthy nations with room to spare turned away desperate guests at their very shores, a refusal now widely remembered as a moral failure.
89.tie_back: The kural calls the failure to keep up hospitality poverty in the midst of plenty and a folly found only in fools, and the St. Louis was refused by countries that had ample means to receive it.
89._accuracy_note: A clear documented case of plenty refusing the guest, though it concerns national refugee policy rather than a household's hospitality.

90.event_title: Marian Anderson is refused Constitution Hall and sings at the Lincoln Memorial
90.event: In 1939 the Daughters of the American Revolution, owners of Constitution Hall in Washington, refused to let the celebrated contralto Marian Anderson perform there because she was Black. First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the organisation in protest, and with the help of Interior Secretary Harold Ickes an open-air concert was arranged on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. On Easter Sunday, 9 April 1939, Anderson sang there to an integrated crowd of about 75,000, with millions more listening on the radio.
90.explanation: A great artist was turned away by the very hosts who should have welcomed her, and the snub became a landmark of the civil rights movement.
90.tie_back: The kural says a guest withers at a host's averted face, and the hall's cold refusal of Marian Anderson shows how wounding an unwelcoming reception is.
90._accuracy_note: Next-best only: a famous documented case of a guest turned away, but Anderson did not wither; she triumphed elsewhere, which partly cuts against the kural's image.
